analysis.title: Productivity For The Few: Morgan Stanley Finds Only A Dozen AI-Heavy Industries Now Generate 83% Of US Productivity Growth
key_insights: Morgan Stanley finds that 2.0pp of the 2.4% y/y rise in US output per employee came from 12 high-AI-exposure industries. The other 52 industries (26 medium exposure, 26 low) contributed 0.4pp combined. That makes about 19% of industries roughly 83% of productivity growth. A year earlier the high-AI group contributed 1.4pp and everyone else 1.0pp, so concentration is rising.

BLS Q3 nonfarm productivity rose 3.6% annualized against a 2.7% consensus, and unit labor costs fell 0.7%. The Morgan Stanley breakdown covers output per employee through Q2 (2.4% y/y, down from 3.0% in Q1, about twice the 20-year average pace). Morgan Stanley reads the 2.1% real GDP growth over four quarters as a supply-side impulse and not overheating demand.

Output per employee in the high-AI group has run at roughly 7%-8% y/y over the past year, the mid-AI group has decelerated for two years, and the low-AI group is contracting or near zero. This year's GDP revisions lifted 2023-24 output per employee by 0.3-0.5pp, but the revisions landed in mid-AI industries. Morgan Stanley suspects pandemic-era cost cutting explains them, so the broad-based part of the productivity gain is the older part and is fading.

Industry detail: data processing and internet publishing +27.0% y/y and accelerating, securities and investments +17.6%, publishing (including software) and computer systems design about +9% each. Hospitals +0.3%, construction flat, restaurants and bars +0.9%, food and beverage stores -4.7%, truck transportation -11.4%, general merchandise stores -11.8%. Funds, trusts and other financial vehicles are +66.7% on a volatile series.

Even inside the high-AI group the picture is mixed. Computer manufacturing output per employee went from +13.0% at end-2025 to -1.1% in Q2 as hiring continued while output fell, which weakens the hardware buildout as a source of productivity. Legal services productivity fell 1.8% as output stalled and payrolls rose.

Morgan Stanley's conclusion, unchanged from six months ago, is that the gains reflect capital deepening in AI-related industries from infrastructure investment and not business-process changes across the economy. The article ties this to Apollo's Slok and SocGen's Edwards, who argue that strong output per hour with flat total factor productivity is capital deepening and not a technology shock, and that AI has delivered no margin boost outside tech.

Goldman's AI Adoption Tracker shows large productivity effects where generative AI is deployed but only modest economy-wide effects. Academic studies imply a 23% average uplift and company anecdotes about 32%. Only 24.6% of US establishments use AI in regular business functions, with adoption near 50% in information, professional and finance sectors. The adoption pattern matches the industries leading Morgan Stanley's productivity table.

Goldman's baseline assumes a 15% AI-driven labor productivity uplift over the adoption period and labor productivity growth averaging about 2.3% over 2026-2030. The article argues this is hard to deliver if half the economy is stuck below 1% productivity growth and the bottom quarter is shrinking.

Morgan Stanley now sees some labor replacement it did not see six months ago. Employment is declining in about half of high-AI industries, with data processing, software and credit intermediation shedding jobs while output rises (credit intermediation may partly reflect a weak housing market). Morgan Stanley calls the effect more micro than macro for now. Goldman counts 207K AI-attributed layoffs since May 2023, and Hatzius sees a significant link between higher AI adoption and weaker employment in nonmanufacturing industries.

Mid- and low-AI industries, which employ most Americans, show stalled employment growth and slowing or negative output growth. The labor share of nonfarm business output fell to 53.0% in Q3, the lowest since the series began in 1947, so productivity gains are not accruing to workers.

Policy angle: the article says concentrated gains in data processing, software and securities do little for prices in the low-AI parts of the CPI basket (groceries, trucking, healthcare). It says Fed Chair Warsh has floated folding AI disinflation into forecasts, that the idea has been delayed, that he hiked in September, and that the jobs report put a December hike back on the table. Morgan Stanley was skeptical of an 'AI = rate cuts' shortcut earlier.

Capex angle: if measured gains are mostly the buildout showing up in the output of the building industries, they depend on capex growth. Hatzius has warned the AI investment impulse peaks around the turn of the year. The author's bet is that concentration persists until the capex cycle rolls over, leaving the economy with the debt and without broad diffusion.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Beat the 2.7% consensus. Morgan Stanley's breakdown shows nearly all the underlying gain comes from high-AI industries, so the headline overstates broad productivity improvement.
Consensus estimate that the 3.6% print beat.
Falling unit labor costs alongside strong productivity support a disinflation read, but the article argues the benefit is concentrated in sectors that do not drive the CPI basket.
Down from 3.0% in Q1 and about twice the 20-year average pace. 2.0pp of it came from 12 high-AI industries.
Morgan Stanley reads it as a supply-side impulse from faster productivity, not overheating demand.

macro_indicators.indicator: Labor share of nonfarm business output
macro_indicators.interpretation: Lowest since the series began in 1947. Productivity gains are going to capital, not workers.
Described as a blowout. Morgan Stanley uses the strong labor market to explain why AI labor replacement is still micro, and the print put a December Fed hike back on the table.
Hard to reach if half the economy sits below 1% productivity growth and the bottom quarter contracts.
Baseline that assumes broad diffusion of AI across industries.

risk_factors: AI gains stay concentrated in a dozen industries, so the economy-wide productivity payoff that the capex and debt funding assume does not arrive.
A roll-over in AI capex, which Goldman's Hatzius sees peaking around the turn of the year, would take down the high-AI output surge that produces most measured productivity growth.
Computer manufacturing output per employee has already fallen from +13.0% to -1.1%, a sign the hardware buildout contribution is fading.
Rising labor replacement in high-AI industries (about half are cutting jobs) and 207K AI-attributed layoffs could weaken the labor market if the broader economy stops absorbing displaced workers.
A record-low labor share of 53.0% means productivity gains are not reaching workers.
Low-AI industries, which employ most Americans, show stalled employment and weak output, leaving productivity flat to falling in the CPI categories that matter for inflation.

tension_points.bull_case: Morgan Stanley stresses productivity growth is about twice the 20-year average and that real GDP growth reflects a supply-side impulse. Optimists say diffusion takes time, as electricity and IT took a decade or more to show up in aggregate data. Morgan Stanley's own summary calls the driver faster output growth with labor displacement a distant secondary role.
tension_points.bear_case: 12 high-AI industries produce 2.0pp of the 2.4% gain, the high-AI share is rising, mid-AI productivity is decelerating and low-AI is contracting. Morgan Stanley and the article see capital deepening from AI infrastructure investment, not business-process change across the economy. Only 24.6% of US establishments use AI.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Mid-AI productivity growth continuing to decelerate and low-AI staying near zero while the AI capex impulse peaks around the turn of the year (Goldman's Hatzius) would invalidate the broad-diffusion case.

tension_points.bull_case: Morgan Stanley says the effect is more micro than macro. The labor market is strong enough to absorb displaced workers, and 165K payrolls backs that up. Productivity growth driven by output is better than growth driven by layoffs.
tension_points.bear_case: Employment is now declining in about half of high-AI industries, including data processing, software and credit intermediation. Goldman counts 207K AI-attributed layoffs and finds a significant link between AI adoption and weaker employment in nonmanufacturing industries. Morgan Stanley says labor replacement is a more evident threat than six months ago.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Employment declines spreading beyond high-AI industries, or the broader labor market ceasing to absorb displaced workers, would invalidate the micro-not-macro view.
